definition: AForge.NET is a computer vision and artificial intelligence library originally developed by Andrew Kirillov for the .NET Framework.
details: The source code and binaries of the project are available under the terms of the Lesser GPL and the GPL (GNU General Public License). Another (unaffiliated) project called Accord.NET was created to extend the features of the original AForge.NET library.

explainer.lead: AForge.NET is a free, open-source toolkit that lets .NET developers add computer vision, neural networks, and robotics control to their applications without starting from scratch. It bundles ready-made code for seeing through cameras, teaching simple artificial brains, and even driving Lego robots, all under the same roof.

tiers.eli5: Imagine you want to build a robot that can follow a red ball with its eyes. Instead of inventing eye-sight from nothing, AForge.NET is like a big box of pre-built robot parts: special eyes that spot colors, a tiny brain that learns from examples, and wheels that connect to Lego kits. You snap the pieces together in your computer program.
tiers.practitioner: AForge.NET targets the .NET Framework and distributes under LGPL/GPL dual licensing, making it viable for both commercial and open-source projects. Typical use involves referencing its DLLs to apply image filters, run back-propagation on multi-layer perceptrons, or control Lego Mindstorms NXT/RCX via Bluetooth or USB. Pitfalls include its 2013 end-of-life: new projects should evaluate Accord.NET, which absorbed AForge.NET's codebase from version 3.0 onward and continues active maintenance.
tiers.paperLevel: AForge.NET implements multi-layer feedforward and distance neural networks with training via back-propagation, delta rule, simple perceptron, and evolutionary learning algorithms. The framework also provides genetic algorithms, genetic programming, gene expression programming, and fuzzy logic inference systems. Originated by Andrew Kirillov; no peer-reviewed foundational paper is named in available sources. Known limit: public support ceased in 2012, with final release 2013.

explainer.example: A developer builds a security camera program that detects motion: they use AForge.NET's video processing to capture frames, apply a difference filter to highlight changes between frames, threshold the result to ignore noise, and trigger an alert when significant movement exceeds a set pixel count.

usedIn.name: Accord.NET
usedIn.detail: Unaffiliated successor project that incorporated AForge.NET's source code from release 3.0 in 2015 and extended its capabilities.

usedIn.name: Research software
usedIn.detail: A number of software applications and research works utilized the framework for computer vision and machine learning experiments.

usedIn.name: Lego Mindstorms robotics
usedIn.detail: Hobbyist and educational projects using NXT and RCX kits with .NET-based control programs.
